---
title: "Calibration"
pagetitle: "TraceGym — judge calibration"
---

An LLM judge is only useful if you know how far to trust it. TraceGym measures
that instead of assuming it.

## The ladder

Cohen's κ is reported next to raw agreement and PABAK, because κ is punished by
the pass-heavy class balance of real agent outputs. The action is pre-decided, so
there is no room to fudge a number:

::: {.metric-grid}
::: {.metric}
[κ ≥ 0.70]{.metric-value}[Judge gates in CI]{.metric-label}
:::
::: {.metric}
[0.55 – 0.70]{.metric-value}[Iterate, gate on the agreement subset]{.metric-label}
:::
::: {.metric}
[κ < 0.55]{.metric-value}[Advisory only, never blocks CI]{.metric-label}
:::
:::

## Confidence and human review

The ensemble reports its own confidence. When the two cross-family judges
disagree, a verdict fails to parse, or a score sits on the threshold, the case is
routed to **NEEDS_REVIEW** rather than forced to pass or fail. That is the honest
alternative to a confident wrong verdict.

## Missing and late labels

Labels are optional and may arrive late. With too few labels or weak agreement,
the judge degrades to advisory and the gate falls back to the deterministic L1
checks, rather than blocking a merge on missing evidence. Nothing is fabricated.

::: {.callout-honest}
**On the demo's numbers.** The bundled demo runs at $0 with a deterministic local
judge and calibrates against a small set of canary golds, an illustrative drift
check. A real Cohen's κ needs your human labels against a live cross-family
judge: run `tg label` to label a stratified sample, then `tg calibrate`. The
harness ships the protocol; the honest number is yours to produce.
:::

## Drift canaries

A meta-judge suite of fixed answers with known verdicts monitors judge and rubric
drift. A `rubric_integrity` check pins the rubric's hash, so tampering with the
rubric is caught deterministically, without a single API call.
